analysis.title: US Economic Notes: What you need to know for the week ahead
key_insights: Chair Warsh opens the week Monday at noon, moderating a panel where the first of his five task forces (productivity and jobs) presents findings at a San Francisco conference. Warsh is unlikely to discuss near-term monetary policy there.
12 other Fed officials appear this week. DB will watch them for changes to policy outlook after last week's stronger than expected inflation data.
The October FOMC minutes are due Wednesday. DB calls them somewhat stale given the October CPI report but a useful benchmark for how policy views have evolved.
After the October CPI report, DB revised up its Fed tightening expectations. It now projects 25bps hikes at each of the next three meetings, taking the fed funds rate to 4.6% by end of Q1 2027.
DB's rates strategy team has also revised its Treasury curve forecasts.

APEC summit: Trump is expected to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines. DB expects little new from either meeting, with the China trade détente maintained and no breakthrough on Ukraine/Russia.

The task force is led by Marc Andreessen, Chad Jones and Asha Sharma. DB's baseline is that it will focus on AI lifting productivity to produce strong growth that is not inflationary. It may also cover AI disruption of the labor market and the impact on r-star.

Tuesday's retail sales and industrial production are the main data highlights. DB expects headline retail sales unchanged (vs +0.8% prior) on weaker auto sales, with gasoline prices dragging ex-autos sales to +0.3% (vs +0.8%).
DB expects retail control sales of +0.4% (vs +0.1%), pointing to still healthy consumer demand. Control is the series used to benchmark goods spending in GDP.
DB expects October industrial production headline of +0.2% (vs +0.7%), slowed by utility output. Higher manufacturing hours worked in the October jobs report point to healthy factory activity.

Recent inflation data show broad-based gains, reinforcing DB's earlier concern about persistent price pressure. Labor data raise the risk that further tightening lets wages re-emerge as an inflation source.

Financial conditions have tightened in recent weeks. A reassessment of AI-related valuations has widened credit spreads and pushed equities lower. DB says this is not yet enough to replace the need for hikes, but a larger and longer extension could make the Fed pause on quickening the pace of hikes.

macro_indicators.interpretation: DB expects continued tightening after the hot October CPI. Rate-sensitive assets stay exposed to further hikes.
Lower auto sales weigh on the headline.
Gasoline prices drag on the ex-auto figure.
Points to still healthy consumer demand growth. This is the series used to benchmark goods spending in GDP.
Utility output slows the headline. Manufacturing hours worked point to healthy factory activity.
Led DB to raise its tightening forecast. No figure is given in this note.

risk_factors: Further Fed tightening could bring wages back as an inflation source.
Tighter financial conditions from an AI valuation reassessment (wider credit spreads, lower equities) could make the Fed pause on quickening hikes.
Elevated geopolitical risk around the APEC meetings.
Possible AI-driven disruption of the US labor market and an effect on r-star, if the task force covers them.
geopolitical: APEC summit: Trump expected to meet Xi Jinping on the sidelines, with the China trade détente expected to hold.
APEC summit: Trump expected to meet Vladimir Putin, with no expected progress on a Ukraine/Russia peace agreement.
DB's geopolitical strategist Helen Belopolsky has published a November 2026 geopolitical preview, referenced in this note.
